description:
POSIX Access Control Lists (ACLs) are more fine-grained access rights for files and directories. An ACL consists of entries specifying access permissions on an associated object. ACLs can be configured per user, per group or via the effective rights mask.

These permissions apply to an individual user or a group, and use the same as rwx found in regular permissions. 

 

Lets prepare our environment before running acl related commands. Create couple of user accounts
useradd giis
useradd wmuser
These two account will be used with acl commands later. Then format the drive with this command
mkfs.ext3 /dev/xvdb
name: Access Control Lists

description:
Mounting File Systems

Before using ACLs for a file or directory, the partition for the file or directory must be mounted with ACL support. If it is a local ext3 file system, it can mounted with the following command:

mount -t ext3 -o acl device-name partition
For example:
mount -t ext3 -o acl /dev/xvdb /mnt
Alternatively, if the partition is listed in the /etc/fstab file, the entry for the partition can include the acl option:

 

LABEL=/mnt      /mnt       ext3    acl        1 2
name: Mounting File Systems

description:
Setting Access ACLs

There are two types of ACLs: access ACLs and default ACLs. An access ACL is the access control list for a specific file or directory. A default ACL can only be associated with a directory; if a file within the directory does not have an access ACL, it uses the rules of the default ACL for the directory. Default ACLs are optional.
ACLs can be configured:
  1. Per user
  2. Per group
  3. Via the effective rights mask
  4. For users not in the user group for the file
The setfacl utility sets ACLs for files and directories. Use the -m option to add or modify the ACL of a file or directory:
setfacl -m rules files
Rules (rules) must be specified in the following formats. Multiple rules can be specified in the same command if they are separated by commas.
u:uid:perms
Sets the access ACL for a user. The user name or UID may be specified. The user may be any valid user on the system.
g:gid:perms
Sets the access ACL for a group. The group name or GID may be specified. The group may be any valid group on the system.
m:perms
Sets the effective rights mask. The mask is the union of all permissions of the owning group and all of the user and group entries.
o:perms
Sets the access ACL for users other than the ones in the group for the file.
Permissions (perms) must be a combination of the characters r, w, and x for read, write, and execute.
If a file or directory already has an ACL, and the setfacl command is used, the additional rules are added to the existing ACL or the existing rule is modified.

Lets create couple of files
touch /mnt/f{1,2}

For example, to give read and write permissions to user giis:
setfacl -m u:giis:rw /mnt/f1
Retrieving ACLs
To determine the existing ACLs for a file or directory, use the getfacl command. In the example below, the getfacl is used to determine the existing ACLs for a file.
getfacl /mnt/f1 
The above command returns the following output:
# file: mnt/f1                                                                  
# owner: root                                                                   
group: root                                                                   
user::rw-                                                                       
user:giis:rw-                                                                   
group::r--                                                                      
mask::rw-                                                                       
other::r--

Lets provide another "wmuser" Read-Write access to this same file. 

setfacl -m u:wmuser:rw /mnt/f1

now verify its permissions again with getfacl you will get output like 

		
# file: mnt/f1                                                                  
# owner: root                                                                   
# group: root                                                                   
user::rw-                                                                       
user:giis:rw-                                                                   
user:wmuser:rw-                                                                 
group::r--                                                                      
mask::rw-                                                                       
other::r--
 

As you can see both users giis and wmuser are provided rights to this file.
name: Setting/Listing Access ACL

description:
Removing ACLs

To remove all the permissions for a user, group, or others, use the -x option and do not specify any permissions:
setfacl -x rules files
For example, to remove all permissions from the user giis:
setfacl -x giis /mnt/f1

now verify its permissions again with getfacl you will get output without user giis

# file: mnt/f1                                                                  
# owner: root                                                                   
# group: root                                                                   
user::rw-                                                                       
user:wmuser:rw-                                                                 
group::r--                                                                      
mask::rw-                                                                       
other::r--
name: Removing Access ACLs

description:
Setting Default ACLs

To set a default ACL, add d: before the rule and specify a directory instead of a file name.
Lets create a directory and set the default.
mkdir /mnt/shares

setfacl -m d:o:rx /mnt/shares
Directories can have a default ACL, which defines the access permissions that files under the directory inherit when they are created. A default ACL affects subdirectories as well as files.

Retrieving Default ACLs

getfacl /mnt/shares/

getfacl: Removing leading '/' from absolute path names
# file: mnt/shares/
# owner: root
# group: root
user::rwx
group::r-x
other::r-x
default:user::rwx
default:group::r-x
default:other::r-x
Note above permission, If you create new child directory /mnt/shares/d1 ,it will inherit the default ACL permissions of the parent directory.Compare below output with previous one
getfacl /mnt/shares/d1
getfacl: Removing leading '/' from absolute path names
# file: mnt/shares/d1
# owner: root
# group: root
user::rwx
group::r-x
other::r-x
default:user::rwx
default:group::r-x
default:other::r-x
name: Set/List Default ACL

description:
Compress/Copy with ACL

When archiving a file or file system with tar, use the --acls option to preserve ACLs. Similarly, when using cp to copy files with ACLs, include the --preserve=mode option to ensure that ACLs are copied across too. Remember we created /mnt/f2 with acl? lets reuse that file

cp /mnt/f2 /mnt/cp_cmd.txt

cp --preserve=mode /mnt/f1 /mnt/cp_cmd2.txt
get the acl from these two files via command
getfacl /mnt/cp_cmd.txt
and
getfacl /mnt/cp_cmd2.txt
I'll let you to find the difference in above two outputs.

Adding a Group to an ACL

The utility setfacl is used to add the groups giis and wmuser to the ACL for the directory /mnt/shares
setfacl -m g:giis:rwx /mnt/shares

setfacl -m g:wmuser:rwx /mnt/shares
Please verify the above changes using getfacl command

Removing a Group from an ACL

The option -x removes groups or users from a given ACL. Below, the group wmuser is removed from the directory /mnt/shares.
setfacl -x g:wmuser /mnt/shares
again, please verify the above changes using getfacl command

Set ACL attributes using a specification file

Lets first, create a file containing the ACL to be used.
echo "g:giis:rwx" > acl
Then, read the contents of the file into setfacl to set the ACL for directory /mnt/shares/d1
setfacl -M acl /mnt/shares/d1

getfacl /mnt/shares/d1
getfacl: Removing leading '/' from absolute path names
# file: mnt/shares/d1
# owner: root
# group: root
user::rwx
group::r-x
group:giis:rwx
mask::rwx
other::r-x
default:user::rwx
default:group::r-x
default:other::r-x
Feel free to play around with acl
